text.title: Content Refresh SOP Core Rules
text.summary: 9 testable rules every Content Refresh SOP application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: Only URLs tagged evergreen with `url_age_months >= 12` enter the scoring matrix. News, dated announcements, release notes and campaign landing pages are excluded from the refresh queue regardless of traffic decline.

rationale.source: Animalz, content decay research; Google Search Central, 'Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content'

rule.rationale: A page under a year old has not lived through one full seasonal cycle, so its impressions curve cannot be separated from launch effects and seasonality; scoring it produces a `kill` verdict for a page that is simply young. Dated content decays by design, and refreshing a 2024 conference recap inflates the queue without recoverable traffic behind it.

rule.statement: Every scored URL row MUST carry, over the same trailing window and the equivalent prior window: Search Console clicks, impressions and average position; GA4 sessions and key events with the URL as landing page; and rank-tracker position for the page's target query. A verdict computed from a single source is invalid. Because the Search Console UI keeps 16 months of performance data, any comparison wider than that MUST read from a persisted export (bulk data export or scheduled API pull), not from the UI.

rationale.source: Google Search Console Help, 'Performance report'; Google Search Central, 'Bulk data export'

rule.rationale: GSC alone shows impressions falling but cannot tell whether the page still converts; GA4 alone shows sessions falling but cannot tell whether the query itself is disappearing. A page that lost 40 percent of impressions because the query volume dropped is a `leave`, not a `refresh`; only the rank-tracker column exposes that. Teams that compare 12 months to the prior 12 months from the UI silently compare 12 months to 4 and call it a trend.

rule.statement: The verdict MUST be derived from three named signals, each with a numeric threshold written into the artefact before scoring: impressions trend (period-over-period percentage change), top-position decay (change in average position for the page's top queries), and intent shift (change in the query mix or SERP features for the target query). An artefact whose decision_branches do not state the thresholds is invalid.

rationale.source: Ahrefs, content decay research; widely established practice in SEO content operations

rule.rationale: Without written thresholds the matrix collapses into editor taste, and the same page gets `refresh` from one reviewer and `leave` from the next. Intent shift is the signal most often skipped: a how-to page whose query now returns product listings cannot be rescued by rewriting, and a refresh spends a writer-week to confirm it.

rule.statement: Every URL that enters the matrix MUST receive exactly one verdict from the closed set `refresh`, `consolidate`, `kill`, `leave`. `leave` is a positive decision recorded with its reason and a next-review date; no URL exits the scoring unclassified or tagged "later".

rationale.source: Widely established practice in content audit operations

rule.rationale: An unclassified URL is re-scored every cycle at full cost and never acted on. Recording `leave` with a reason is what lets the next audit skip it in seconds instead of re-pulling three data sources for a page nobody intends to touch.

rule.statement: A `consolidate` verdict MUST name the single surviving canonical URL, list every merged URL, and specify a 301 (or 308) redirect from each merged URL to the survivor, plus the rewrite of every internal link that pointed at a merged URL. Merging content and deleting the source pages without redirects is forbidden.

rationale.source: Google Search Central, 'Redirects and Google Search'

rule.rationale: Permanent redirects are the strongest signal Google accepts that the merged page's ranking signals now belong to the survivor; without them the backlinks and query history of the deleted pages are simply lost and the survivor starts from zero. The typical incident is a cluster of five thin posts merged into one guide, the five deleted, and organic traffic for the topic falling below the pre-merge total.

rule.statement: A `kill` verdict MUST make the URL return 410 Gone (404 is acceptable), remove it from the XML sitemap and from internal navigation, and drop inbound internal links. A killed URL MUST NOT be redirected to the homepage or to an unrelated hub page; redirect only when a genuinely equivalent page exists, in which case the verdict is `consolidate`.

rationale.source: Google Search Console Help, 'Soft 404 errors'; Google Search Central, 'HTTP status codes, network and DNS errors'

rule.rationale: Google treats a redirect from a specific page to the homepage as a soft 404, so the "keep the link equity" trick buys nothing and adds a Search Console error class to monitor. Leaving killed pages in the sitemap keeps them crawled and reported as errors for months.

rule.statement: A `refresh` MUST keep the URL unchanged. `dateModified` in structured data and the visible byline date MUST be updated only when the substantive body content changed; bumping the date on a page with no material edit is forbidden. Title and H1 may change only to match the current query intent recorded in the intent-shift signal.

rationale.source: Google Search Central, guidance on page dates and structured data; Google Search Central, 'Redirects and Google Search'

rule.rationale: Renaming the slug during a refresh converts a refresh into a migration: every backlink now hits a redirect and the page is re-evaluated from scratch. Date-only bumps are the most common fake refresh; Google's guidance explicitly asks not to update the date without significant new information, and readers who notice a "2026" date on 2021 screenshots stop trusting the whole domain.

rule.statement: A `refresh` MUST execute all nine checklist steps, each with an exit criterion recorded in the artefact's steps array: (1) re-run query and intent research for the target query; (2) update every fact, statistic, price and date with a dated source; (3) rewrite title, meta description and intro to the current intent; (4) add or replace sections for subtopics the top-ranking pages cover and this page does not; (5) refresh screenshots, media and examples; (6) update internal links in and out, including links from newer pages; (7) fix technical issues found on the URL (broken links, missing alt text, structured-data errors, Core Web Vitals failures); (8) update `dateModified` and append a changelog entry; (9) request re-indexing and record the baseline snapshot. A refresh that skips a step MUST record which step and why in the deviation log.

rationale.source: Widely established practice in SEO content operations; Google Search Central, 'Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content'

rule.rationale: A "refresh" that only edits the intro and the date is the pattern behind refreshes that produce no measurable lift. Steps 4 and 6 are the ones that move rankings and the ones most often skipped because they take the longest; making every step an explicit exit criterion is what turns the SOP from advice into a checklist a reviewer can fail.

rule.statement: Every `refresh` and `consolidate` MUST record a baseline snapshot (clicks, impressions, average position, GA4 sessions and key events for the trailing 28 days) on the day of publication, and MUST schedule a re-evaluation at day 90 that re-scores the URL against that baseline and the same thresholds. A URL with no baseline cannot be declared a success or a failure.

rationale.source: Google Search Central, 'Ask Google to recrawl your URLs'; widely established practice in SEO content operations

rule.rationale: Re-crawl and re-ranking take days to weeks, and seasonal noise dominates any window shorter than a quarter, so reading results at day 14 rewards and punishes randomly. Without a recorded baseline the 90-day review compares against memory, and the same page is refreshed again the next cycle because nobody can show the last refresh worked.

section.title: Conclusion targets used by the decision tree

rule.statement: Run the full procedure; emit an artefact passing the output contract.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when the URL is eligible and the dataset is complete.

rule.statement: Skip; surface the missing precondition; do not synthesize.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when the URL is not eligible for the refresh matrix.
